source.title: Towards Understanding Generalization via Decomposing Excess Risk Dynamics
source.authors: Jia-Ye Teng; Jian-Hao Ma; Yang Yuan

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including supplementary material; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents reading.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports neural-network experiments that measure how excess risk decomposes into signal and noise components during training, a related generalization-dynamics property. It does not test the listed versions' accuracy gaps, width effects, optimizer or batch comparisons, regularization effects, sharpness rankings, or memorized-example removal.
record.gate_note: The neural-network experiments report excess-risk decomposition and a Dynamics Decomposition Condition, rather than held-out accuracy or the training-to-test error gap specified by the listed versions. These results bear on the claim's generalization subject but fit none of V1–V8. The paper also cites results from prior work; those citations are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests an excess-risk decomposition framework, not V1–V8. Width and optimizer experiments assess decomposition bounds rather than comparative generalization performance. Random-label experiments do not establish near-perfect training fit alongside natural-label held-out accuracy.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors propose separating signal and noise excess-risk dynamics, applying stability to the noise component and uniform convergence to the signal component. They derive improved bounds for linear regression and diagonal matrix recovery and present neural-network experiments illustrating the framework. The neural-network evidence does not establish any of V1–V8.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes a theoretical excess-risk decomposition and tests the decomposition property in neural-network experiments; it does not reproduce the original empirical interventions or measures in V1–V8.
record.method_sensitivity: The decomposition-bound success constant changes with depth and width in the synthetic experiment; the authors state it becomes large with increasing depth and that decomposition works better as width increases. Optimizers SGD, Adam, and Rprop yield different reported constants in the same synthetic experiment. On CIFAR-10, the authors report variance-training behavior different from MNIST.

fits_no_version.finding: Synthetic and MNIST experiments qualitatively show excess risk following the bias component early and the variance component later.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Excess-risk dynamics admit an approximate signal/noise decomposition in the tested neural-network settings.

fits_no_version.finding: The plotted DDC upper bound exceeds the prediction-function distance in synthetic neural-network experiments at n = 500 and n = 1500.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested neural-network trajectories satisfy the illustrated decomposition condition in function space.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors illustrate decomposition bounds using chosen multipliers that increase with depth, decrease with width, and remain small across three optimizers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The empirical adequacy of the proposed decomposition varies with architecture and extends across the tested optimizers.

fits_no_version.finding: CIFAR-10 variance training approaches the uniform-label population optimum in the illustrated setting; other learning-rate regimes overfit and produce VER approximately 10.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Random-label population-risk dynamics for ResNet-18 depend on the learning-rate regime.

record.problems: The neural-network evidence for the central decomposition property is mainly presented in figures; the main text gives qualitative descriptions, and no numeric uncertainty is supplied for the Figure 2/3 results. Appendix A reports five trials and standard-deviation error bars but does not state numeric error bars in the text. The experiments assess decomposition properties rather than the train-test error gap in the catalog versions.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying results omitted. Theoretical bounds and comparisons for linear regression and diagonal matrix recovery do not test a listed claim version and are not rows for the neural-network finding catalog.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fixed-random-label training fit together with natural-label held-out accuracy above chance and random-label held-out accuracy at chance under the same recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Matched convolutional versus fully connected image-classification performance and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD held-out performance under specified tuning budgets and recovery recipes.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove the penalty.
Dropout interventions and their effects on held-out error.
Magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation tolerance and its ranking of train-test gaps.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: T6 concerns the listed versions, despite the paper's substantive contribution to generalization theory. Its local sharpness factor describes excess-risk scaling near a minimizer, not V7's magnitude-aware perturbation measure. No qualifying version-specific result is missing.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label held-out accuracy coexistence.
Test error as width increases beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier test error and architectural bias.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD held-out performance.
Large-batch generalization gap and recipe adaptations.
Magnitude-aware sharpness as a measure tracking the train-test gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.

relation.reason: The paper discusses generalization and signal-versus-noise fitting while testing its own decomposition framework, without testing a listed claim version.

tranche.reason: The study develops and evaluates excess-risk decomposition bounds. Its width, optimizer, and noisy-label experiments do not establish any V1–V8 effect.

source_check.notes: The authors-conclusion paraphrase is accurate. Appendix A.2 footnote 10 qualifies the CIFAR-10 result: some learning-rate regimes overfit random labels and yield VER approximately 10; the reported standard deviations concern the plotted dynamics, not uncertainty estimates for a.
